judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Clipped, practical handoff with a gift and a 'lad'. The odd phrase 'heed its bite' and the bare, gruff reminder sound like Westwood's own lines.

items.label: B
items.critique: Stock fantasy setup (bandit chief, cutthroats, honest folk, crossroads) that reads like a generic RPG quest-giver. The last page just restates the route, which feels written to make sure the player knows where to go.

items.label: C
items.critique: Long and expository, with spies, letters and a two-target briefing. The agreement slip ('Robberies ... is') looks like an imitated flaw, and the reminder brings up a horn the opening never named.

items.label: D
items.critique: Has the right brusque energy and the 'last hope' close, but 'king of the Trolls' and the stacked [Place] of [Place] read like a pastiche of the mine-handoff pattern.

items.label: E
items.critique: 'You'll see.' is a non sequitur, and the reminder says the objective twice ('learn if the stories are true', 'see if he has already been there'). The pit warning is a nice touch, but the line doesn't flow the way Westwood's do.

items.label: F
items.critique: Stiff, formal self-introduction ('The Master for the...'), capitalised 'YOU' and a key handed over. That clumsy-but-earnest ceremony is how Westwood writes late-game exposition.

items.label: G
items.critique: The reasoning is tangled ('With Ghosts on the loose ... [Person] is certainly behind all of this'), and 'put your feet up' plus the stacked theft backstory feel like a pastiche of Westwood's exclamatory handoffs.

items.label: H
items.critique: Sounds like Jandor's arrival speech: grand dashes and exclamations, 'test of your life', and a deadpan 'It weeds out the weak recruits.'

items.label: I
items.critique: Wry opening apology ('Sorry about the stench, lad'), a concrete count of guards, and a reminder that explains how to use the spells. Very Nox.

items.label: J
items.critique: Breathless '!?' and exclamation marks, the clunky 'leaving rebuilding the village our smallest concern' and 'All Nox is now in peril'. That overwrought urgency is Westwood's.

tells: Westwood's openers are short and in medias res: one concrete detail of the place (a stench, too many eyes, a weeding-out test), then the order. The new ones explain the backstory and politics (letters, spies, two objectives).
Generic fantasy stock (bandit chief, cutthroats, honest folk, dark times at the crossroads) separates the new texts from Nox's specific, slightly odd world.
Westwood's reminders are curt and impatient ('Go! Don't just stand there.') or hand over one practical tip. The new ones repeat the objective or bring in details not set up before.
Pastiches overdo Westwood's tics: stacked masked nouns, 'lad', exclamations and imitated grammar slips, while their cause-and-effect turns muddled ('You'll see.', 'is certainly behind all of this').
